title: Women among the five
hook: some gurdwaras include women among the Panj Pyare, some do not, and Sikhs discuss it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Dasam Granth question: views differ on who wrote parts of it, but both sides recite Jaap Sahib and Chaupai in the daily prayers. Your line was shared devotion. What did you find you both still love? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-five.

An amrit ceremony, in a closed room. Five initiated Sikhs in saffron stand around an iron bowl of water, stirring it with a double-edged khanda while they recite. They are the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones, standing in for the first five who answered the Guru's call. In one city, one of the five today is a woman. In another city, at another gurdwara, the five are always men. Both are Sikh ceremonies. Today is the conversation between them.
screen: `FIVE IN SAFFRON, ONE IRON BOWL.` → `IN ONE CITY, A WOMAN AMONG THEM.` → `IN ANOTHER, ALWAYS MEN.`

segments.voice: Begin with the story. Tradition says that at Anandpur, Guru Gobind Singh asked the gathered Sikhs who would give their head, and five men stepped forward one by one. They became the first Panj Pyare and received the first amrit. Tradition also says that Mata Sahib Kaur came and added sugar sweets to the water, so that the amrit would carry sweetness along with the steel. So the first five were men, and a woman's hand is in the bowl. Here's where the views part. Some Sikhs hold that the five should follow the first five, and that the ceremony keeps its shape best by keeping its history. Others point to the Sikh code of conduct, whose readers say its section on the amrit ceremony allows Sikh women to be among the five. And they point to a line from the Asa di Var that this path met on the phulkari day. On Ang 473, Guru Nanak asks, here in paraphrase, why call her lesser, from whom kings are born? Here it's read as a question about who may stand at the bowl. In practice, some gurdwaras now include women among the Panj Pyare, and some do not. Both sides take the ceremony seriously, which is exactly why they care. The disagreement is not about whether amrit matters. It's about how faithfully to keep a picture of the first day, and what faithfulness asks. Sikhs keep discussing it in gurdwara committees, in homes and online, and meanwhile the ceremony is held both ways.
screen: `FIVE MEN STEPPED FORWARD.` · `A WOMAN'S HAND IN THE BOWL.` · `THE CODE AND ANG 473.` · `TWO PRACTICES, ONE CEREMONY.` · then, large: `WHAT DOES FAITHFULNESS ASK?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice an open conversation. Settle, and breathe. Think of a conversation in your own life that isn't finished. In your family, your work, your faith community, your neighborhood. Don't try to win it, and don't try to end it. Just notice where it lives: at a dinner table, in a message thread, in your own head late at night. Notice whether it's still being held kindly. Then think of the next time it will come up, and choose one small thing that would keep it open: a question, a pause, a cup of tea. Breathe with that choice for a while. The bell holds the time.
Women among the five. Some gurdwaras include women among the Panj Pyare who serve amrit, some do not, and Sikhs are still talking it through. Today's word.

Your line: the conversation continues. Today, when a discussion ends without agreement, let it end kindly, and leave the door open with one sentence like: let's keep talking. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-five.
